what: GIF Maker turns a series of pictures into an animated GIF. Add two or more images, arrange them in order, choose how long each frame shows, and get a GIF that plays in any browser, chat app or email.

You can set the width, the shape, how pictures of different shapes fit, how many times it loops, and add a caption on every frame. A live preview shows the animation before you create it, and the finished file size is shown so you can keep it small enough to share.
The GIF is encoded in a background worker in your browser; nothing is uploaded.
uses: Turn a few drawings or photos into a flip-book style animation.
Cycle through several product photos or a before and after pair.
Show the steps of a process as frames in one small GIF for docs or support replies.
Add a caption like Happy birthday! across a few photos.
Share a handful of pictures as one looping animation.
tutorial: Click "Click or drop images here" and choose two or more images. Each becomes a frame in the list.
Drag a frame by ⠿ to a new place, or use the ↑ and ↓ buttons. Click ✕ to remove a frame.

Type a "Time per frame" in milliseconds, for example 500 for half a second. Untick "Same time for every frame" to type a different time for each frame. Choose Loop forever, Play once or a number of plays under "Repeat".
Pick the width and the shape. If your pictures have different shapes, choose whether to fit the whole picture with bars, fill and crop, or stretch.
Type a caption, choose top, middle or bottom, and set its size and colour.
Watch the preview, then click "Create GIF". The file size, number of frames and length are shown with the finished GIF. Click Download.
features: Reorder frames by dragging, or with arrow buttons on touch screens.
From 20 ms to 10 seconds per frame.
Loop forever, play once, or play 2, 3 or 5 times.
240 to 1080 px wide, original, square, 4:3, 16:9 or 9:16, with fit, fill or stretch.
Bold outlined text that reads on any picture.
See the animation before you encode it and the size after.
Uses the open-source gifenc encoder in a worker, so the page stays responsive.

example.title: Worked example: a 4-photo birthday GIF
example.text: Nadia adds four party photos, drags the cake photo to the end and sets the time per frame to 700 ms. She chooses 480 px, Square, Fill and crop, types Happy birthday Sam! at the bottom, and leaves Repeat on Loop forever. She clicks Create GIF and gets a 480 × 480 GIF of 4 frames, 2.8 s long and about 350 KB, small enough to send in any chat app.

tips: 100 to 200 ms per frame looks like motion; 500 ms or more feels like a slideshow.
Give the last frame a longer time so viewers can read it before the loop restarts.
Keep GIFs for chats under about 5 MB: use 480 px or less and fewer frames.
Simple graphics and screenshots make much smaller GIFs than detailed photos.
GIFs have no sound. For long or detailed clips, a video file is smaller and sharper.
problems: The Create GIF button is greyed out
The GIF looks banded or grainy
GIFs can only use 256 colours per frame. Choose 256 colours, or use pictures with fewer smooth gradients.
The file is too big to send
Lower the width, choose 64 colours, or remove some frames.
It says there are too many pixels
Very large widths with many frames need too much memory. Choose a smaller width or fewer frames.
